doc.title: Artie Shaw — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Amplification and balancing the band for records
summary: Guitar was amplified around 1940 and bass in the late 1940s; the band balanced itself, with brass on risers and one-microphone records.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Did you have any amplification on, say, the bass or the guitar at that time.

No. We didn’t have it in the early days. There wasn’t any. In 19 . . . around 1940, when I got the Gramercy Five thing together out of that string band, yeah, then we began to have at least amplification on guitar. But not on bass. It took many years. 1949 and ’48 was when they began doing that. My 1949 band, I remember the bass player showed up. He had a speaker.
So you were doing something which tends not to be done anymore, which was, the band balanced itself internally.

That too. When you made records, you put the band . . . the brass on risers, trombones on one level, trumpets on the other, so they’d blow over each other instead of each other’s backs, and when the guy had a mute solo, he have to run down. Some of our records were made with one mic. When you had to play, or the singer had to get into the mic . . . You had to get close if you wanted to do something with the singer. If it’s a muted section thing, you had to be very careful to make sure the band played very softly, so the mutes could be heard. Yeah, there was a constant . . . but you were aware of that, that you were doing that, because that was part of the recording process, learning how to make a record.
